summary: This standards-track document defines a new name form in the X.509 Subject Alternative Name and Issuer Alternative Name extensions that ties a certificate subject to an internationalized email address. It updates RFC 5280. It was later replaced by RFC 9598.

eli5.summary: Email names can use letters from many languages. This adds a spot in a digital ID card for such names. It was later replaced by RFC 9598.

questions: how to put an internationalized email address in a certificate
how do i put an international email address in a certificate
how are international email addresses compared in certificates
subtitle: Support for email addresses with non-ASCII characters in digital certificates.

tldr.problem: X.509 certificates can only include ASCII email addresses in the rfc822Name field, leaving out email addresses from non-English-speaking regions that use international characters.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8398 defines a new name form called SmtpUTF8Mailbox in the X.509 otherName field that allows full internationalized email addresses with non-ASCII characters in both the local-part and domain.
tldr.outcome: Certificates can now represent email addresses in any language. RFC 9598 later superseded this with updates to email internationalization handling.

today: RFC 8398 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5280. It was later superseded by RFC 9598, which provides revised procedures for internationalized email addresses in certificates.

sections.title: Email Addresses in Many Languages
sections.content:
RFC 5280 defines X.509 certificates, which are digital ID documents used to prove identity on the internet. One field in a certificate can hold an email address using the rfc822Name form, but it is restricted to ASCII characters only. This works for English email addresses but fails for speakers of other languages who have non-ASCII characters in their email addresses.

RFC 6531 extended SMTP to support internationalized email (SMTPUTf8): email addresses where the local-part (the part before the @) can contain non-ASCII UTF-8 characters, and domain names can contain non-ASCII Unicode. RFC 8398 brings this support to X.509 certificates by defining a new name form, SmtpUTF8Mailbox, that can be placed in the otherName field of a certificate's Subject Alternative Name or Issuer Alternative Name extension.
sections.eli5: This lets a certificate hold an email address with Chinese characters, or accented letters, or any other non-English writing.

sections.title: The SmtpUTF8Mailbox Name Form
sections.content:
SmtpUTF8Mailbox is an otherName variant that stores an internationalized email address as a UTF-8 string. The object identifier is id-on-SmtpUTF8Mailbox (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.8.9).

An internationalized email address has two parts: a local-part (before the @) and a domain (after the @). RFC 8398 specifies:

  • Local-part: Can contain any UTF-8 characters as allowed by RFC 6531, including non-ASCII. The local-part is case-sensitive and must not be normalized or folded in any way.
  • Domain: Must conform to IDNA2008 (RFC 5890). Domain labels containing non-ASCII characters are stored in U-label form (Unicode) rather than A-label form (ASCII-compatible encoding). ASCII-only domain labels must use lowercase NR-LDH (Non-Reserved Letters Digits Hyphen) format.
  • Encoding: SmtpUTF8Mailbox is encoded as UTF8String in ASN.1, without a Byte-Order-Mark.

When a certificate contains an internationalized email with non-ASCII in the local-part, SmtpUTF8Mailbox MUST be used. When the local-part is ASCII-only, the legacy rfc822Name subjectAltName MUST be used instead, ensuring compatibility with older software that does not support SmtpUTF8Mailbox.
sections.eli5: A SmtpUTF8Mailbox is a spot in a certificate that holds an email address with international characters. The local-part can be in any language. The domain must follow IDNA2008 rules.

sections.title: Matching and Comparison Rules
sections.content:
When comparing two SmtpUTF8Mailboxes to check if they are the same address, the comparison has two parts: domain and local-part.

Domain comparison: If the domain contains A-labels (ASCII-compatible encoding like xn--...), they must first be converted to U-labels (Unicode). ASCII-only NR-LDH labels must be converted to lowercase. After this normalization, domains are compared octet-for-octet for exact match.

Local-part comparison: The local-part must conform to RFC 6530 and RFC 6531 rules. It is compared as-is in UTF-8 form without any transformation, case folding, or normalization. This preserves the user's intent.

Setup steps: To compare a SmtpUTF8Mailbox with other email forms (rfc822Name or raw internationalized email addresses):

  1. Remove any surrounding phrases, comments, angle brackets.
  2. Convert domain A-labels to U-labels if present.
  3. Convert ASCII domain NR-LDH labels to lowercase.
  4. For rfc822Name and raw addresses, ensure the local-part is in UTF-8 form.
  5. Compare the resulting strings octet-for-octet.

SmtpUTF8Mailbox does not support wildcard characters. To specify multiple email addresses, use multiple subject alternative name entries.
sections.eli5: When checking if two email addresses are the same, normalize the domain but leave the local-part exactly as written. No wildcards allowed.

sections.title: Name Constraints and Path Validation
sections.content:
X.509 path validation uses name constraints to ensure that a CA certificate is only used to issue certificates for a permitted set of domains or email addresses. RFC 8398 updates RFC 5280 to extend rfc822Name name constraints to also apply to SmtpUTF8Mailbox subject alternative names, since both represent the same email address namespace.

A name constraint for rfc822Name applies to both rfc822Name and SmtpUTF8Mailbox subject alternative names. When validating a SmtpUTF8Mailbox against an rfc822Name name constraint:

  1. Apply the setup steps from the matching rules (convert A-labels, lowercase ASCII labels).
  2. Strip the local-part and @ sign from both, leaving just the domain.
  3. Apply the standard rfc822Name name constraint comparison from RFC 5280.

The RFC notes that name constraints on specific mailboxes (with a local-part) are rarely used and impractical for internationalized addresses. RFC 8399 updates the rules to allow only host-level and domain-level constraints and deprecates mailbox-level constraints.

CAs issuing CA certificates with email address name constraints MUST use rfc822Name only, with IDNA2008-conformant names and non-ASCII domains in A-label form.
sections.eli5: Name constraints tell a CA which email addresses it can issue certificates for. These rules now apply to both old ASCII email and new international email addresses.
